title: Least Variable Quantum Counting Processes
authors: Bita Olamaei, Florian Meier, Costantino Budroni, Pharnam Bakhshinezhad, Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract: Counting processes provide a fundamental description of stochastic events ranging from photon detection to clock ticks. A central question is how accurately such events can be timed when only finite memory resources are available. Here, we investigate this problem within a general framework of finite-dimensional classical and quantum counting processes. We derive a rigorous finite-memory variance bound obeyed by every classical $d$-state counting process, which is tight and saturated by a discrete Erlang-type ladder process. Through numerical optimization, we identify quantum counting processes that violate this classical bound, achieving smaller first-tick fluctuations than any classical process with the same memory size and mean tick time. For the qubit case, we further derive an analytical large-mean bound within a single-Kraus no-tick family, showing that the quantum advantage persists asymptotically within this class. The optimized quantum processes exhibit coherent conditioned dynamics and approach a continuous-time quantum-jump description as the mean increases. Our results establish a finite-memory quantum advantage in temporal precision and connect discrete-time counting processes with continuous-time quantum timekeeping.
summary: This paper establishes a quantum advantage in the temporal precision of counting processes when memory is finite. By deriving rigorous variance bounds for classical counting processes, the authors show that quantum dynamics can surpass these classical limits. This work connects discrete-time quantum measurement theory to continuous-time quantum timekeeping.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental limits on temporal precision (tick timing) when counting stochastic events using finite memory resources, comparing classical and quantum constraints.
main_result: Quantum counting processes can achieve smaller first-tick fluctuations than any classical process with the same memory size and mean tick time, establishing a finite-memory quantum advantage in temporal precision.
method: The authors derive rigorous finite-memory variance bounds for classical counting processes and use numerical optimization and asymptotic analysis to identify quantum processes that violate these classical bounds.
model_or_system: The model involves finite-dimensional classical and quantum counting processes, described by substochastic transition matrices or quantum instruments/Kraus operators, respectively. The analysis covers both discrete-time and continuous-time limits.
key_observables: Variance ($\sigma^2_{dt}$), first-tick probability ($p_L$), hazard rate ($h_L$), and the relative precision measure ($N = \mu^2_{ct} / \sigma^2_{ct}$).
important_parameters: Memory dimension ($d$), mean tick time ($\mu_{dt}$), and the asymptotic limit ($\mu_{dt} 	o \infty$ or $\delta 	o 0^+$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes autonomous machines operating cyclically (renewal processes) and utilizes approximations for large mean times and small time steps ($\delta$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual overview of discrete-time evolution, the waiting time probability distribution for various memory sizes, and the comparison of quantum vs. classical statistics.
paper_structure: The paper develops the classical variance bound, identifies quantum violations via numerical optimization, and then analyzes the asymptotic continuous-time limit, culminating in an analytical solution for the qubit case ($d=2$).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum timekeeping and the fundamental limits of measurement precision, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems theory.
